summary: This document describes a lightweight key management variant for MIKEY (RFC 3830) using Diffie-Hellman key agreement, which gives perfect forward secrecy, together with a keyed hash to provide mutual authentication and message integrity. It targets the security and performance needs of multimedia key management.

eli5.summary: Two people want to agree on a secret code in public without anyone guessing it. They mix their own secrets in a clever way and then check each other's stamp to be sure.

subtitle: Setting up fresh media keys in one round trip using Diffie-Hellman, with a pre-shared secret proving who is who.

tldr.problem: The existing MIKEY key schemes either lack perfect forward secrecy (pre-shared and public-key modes) or need a public-key infrastructure (public-key and signed Diffie-Hellman modes).
tldr.mechanism: Each side sends a Diffie-Hellman half-key in a message protected by an HMAC keyed from a pre-shared secret. Both then compute the same shared key, and no certificates are needed.
tldr.outcome: It gives forward secrecy and mutual authentication in one round trip, but only for two parties. It does not scale to larger groups.

today: RFC 4650 is a Proposed Standard from September 2006. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Another MIKEY Mode
sections.content:
MIKEY (Multimedia Internet KEYing, RFC 3830) already has three peer-to-peer key management schemes that finish in one round trip: a pre-shared key mode (MIKEY-PS), a public-key encryption mode (MIKEY-PK) and a signed Diffie-Hellman mode (MIKEY-DHSIGN). This RFC points out the limits of each.

With pre-shared keys, a compromise of the shared master secret exposes past and future session keys, and the responder must trust the initiator to pick a good session key. The public-key modes depend on a public-key infrastructure, which was not widely available. Checking certificates can also add round trips and delay.

DHHMAC is a fourth mode. It applies the Diffie-Hellman key agreement but authenticates the exchange with a keyed hash and a pre-shared secret instead of a digital signature. It reuses MIKEY payloads and mechanisms as much as possible.
sections.eli5: The old ways either let one person pick the secret alone or needed a big official office to vouch for people. This new way lets two friends build the secret together using a password they already share.

sections.title: Scenario and Applicability
sections.content:
DHHMAC addresses the same scope as the other MIKEY modes. It suits a peer-to-peer setting where no public-key infrastructure is available but the two parties already share a master secret. It assumes at least loosely synchronized clocks, and it defines no secure time synchronization of its own.

It is meant for application-level key management and for call setup protocols with a two-way handshake. The RFC names SIP with SDP, where MIKEY messages ride in the SDP offer/answer, and H.323, where they travel in the H.225.0 fast start handshake.

Because Diffie-Hellman is pairwise and the exchange takes one round trip, DHHMAC cannot serve a group of more than two entities. In the group key management architecture it could only act as a registration protocol in the degenerate two-peer case.
sections.eli5: It is made for two people starting a call who already share a secret. It cannot handle a whole classroom at once.

sections.title: The DHHMAC Exchange
sections.content:
The initiator picks a random secret xi and sends an I_message containing a header, a timestamp, a random value, its optional identity, the responder's identity, optional security policy payloads, its Diffie-Hellman half-key g^(xi) and a KEMAC payload that holds the HMAC. The responder picks xr and answers with an R_message carrying g^(xr), the received half-key and its own HMAC.

Both sides then compute the traffic key generation key (TGK) as g^(xi * xr). The HMAC is computed over the whole message except the MAC field, using an auth_key derived from the pre-shared secret with the MIKEY pseudo-random function. It is what stops man-in-the-middle attacks on the half-keys.

The initiator SHALL always include the recipient's identity. The responder SHALL always include the initiator's identity. The group is sent as an encoding of the Diffie-Hellman group, and the actual parameters are deduced from it. Either side MAY precompute its half-key off-line to cut delay.

Re-keying uses an update message. Fresh half-keys are exchanged for true re-keying. If the Diffie-Hellman payloads are left out, only non-key data such as security policy is updated and the TGK does not change.
sections.eli5: Each friend mixes a private number into a public one and sends it over with a secret seal. When both mix the other's public number with their own private one, they end up with the very same secret.

sections.title: Payload Formats and Codes
sections.content:
This RFC defines no new payload formats. It reuses these MIKEY payloads: HDR, the SRTP ID sub-payload, KEMAC, DH, timestamp, ID, security policy, RAND, error and general extension.

The header data types are 7 for the initiator's DHHMAC message and 8 for the responder's. This is how a responder tells DHHMAC from plain MIKEY. An error message uses 6. The responder SHALL send an error payload on a decoding error or a failed HMAC check.

KEMAC carries only the HMAC here. It conveys no encrypted data, so the encryption algorithm is set to 2 (NULL), and AES key wrap is not used. It MUST be the last payload. HMAC-SHA-1 (value 0, 160-bit result) is the mandatory default. The ID payload holds only non-certificate-based identities.

To prevent bidding-down attacks, the general extension payload lists all key management protocol identifiers of the surrounding protocol, such as SDP. It is integrity protected by the HMAC.
sections.eli5: The notes use the same envelope shapes as before. A number on the envelope says whether it is the first note or the reply, and the seal goes last.

sections.title: Security Properties and Limits
sections.content:
The TGK is never sent on the wire, even encrypted. Only the half-keys are, and eavesdropping on them is not considered a substantial risk. Mutual authentication comes from proving possession of the pre-shared key in both messages. Timestamps give replay protection, which needs roughly synchronized clocks. If sync is lost, replays cannot be detected and keying can fail.

Checking the HMAC is quick, so a message can be verified before the costly Diffie-Hellman work starts. That gives limited denial-of-service protection, not a defence against large distributed attacks. Perfect forward secrecy means a later compromise of the long-term pre-shared key does not expose past or future session keys. Both parties also contribute to the key.

Each party SHALL generate xi or xr with a strong unpredictable generator and keep them private. Destroying them after use is RECOMMENDED.

The RFC says identity protection is not provided. Leaving out identity fields is a protocol optimization, not a privacy method, and it can expose masquerade, impersonation and reflection attacks.

Security rests on stated assumptions: a secret, high-entropy pre-shared key, a secure pseudo-random function, a large Diffie-Hellman group and a secure SHA1 and HMAC. The RFC admits these are neither proven nor disproven, so some residual risk remains.
sections.eli5: The secret code never travels, only the mixed-up halves do. A fast check of the seal also lets you toss out fake notes before doing the hard math. The seal only works as long as the shared password stays secret.

sections.title: Use with H.323 and H.235
sections.content:
Appendix A is informative. It outlines use of MIKEY-DHHMAC in H.323 environments, where the keys then protect media with SRTP. A caller sends the I_message inside the H.323 SETUP, and the called endpoint answers with the R_message in the CallProceeding-to-Connect message. Both endpoints end up with the same TGK.

The endpoints typically do not share an auth_key beforehand. It is set up by some separate exchange while they register with the gatekeeper. For full-duplex calls needing keys in both directions, the caller can run the protocol twice in parallel.
sections.eli5: When one phone calls another, the first note rides along with the ring and the reply comes back when the call is answered. By then both phones hold the same secret.
